title: Gemini for Mac can now use your apps for you. Anthropic’s shares close their first day 17% above the IPO price. ChatGPT gets an accounting plugin, Meta’s Muse agent shows staff chats that are not theirs, big US school districts weigh dropping Google Search over AI, and OpenAI lets Codex agents fix ChatGPT slowdowns.
summary: Google added computer use to the Gemini app for Mac on 19 November: it works in a background window across your apps, files and the web, for paid Google AI plans in the US. Anthropic opened at $111.50 on Nasdaq against its $83 IPO price and closed at $97.17, up 17%, CNBC reports. OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Accounting with plugins for QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite, FreshBooks and others. Reuters reports Meta staff testing Muse saw it surface Signal messages and bank balances that were not theirs; Meta calls them isolated incidents, mostly hallucinations. New York, Los Angeles and Chicago schools are weighing alternatives after Google said schools cannot switch off its AI without losing Search. OpenAI says its Codex-run Performance Factory handled more than 1,700 ChatGPT slowdown investigations in just over three months.
uncertainty: Gemini’s computer use details come from Google’s own post. Anthropic trading figures are CNBC’s; the Nasdaq and share moves are the BBC’s. Customer time savings for ChatGPT for Accounting are customers’ estimates on OpenAI’s page. The Muse examples come from internal posts reviewed by Reuters, which could not establish whether the data was real or made up; Meta says many were hallucinations. The school district positions are as reported by The Verge and The New York Times. Performance Factory figures are OpenAI’s own.

stories.theme: Gemini for Mac can now click, type and fill in forms across your apps, files and the web, in a background window
stories.changed: On 19 November 2026 Google added computer use to the Gemini app for Mac. You describe a task and Gemini navigates menus, types, clicks and fills in forms across your local files, desktop apps and websites to finish it. It works in an isolated background window with a live preview in the chat, so your own screen and cursor stay free while it runs. Google says you choose which apps it can open, can watch every step, pause at any time, and approve key actions before they happen. Google’s examples include batch colour-grading photos, copying weights, sizes and addresses from PDFs into multi-box shipping quote forms, and pulling figures from live dashboards into a Google Slides deck. It is rolling out in English in the US, needs an Apple Silicon Mac on macOS Sequoia 15.0 or later, and is for personal Google accounts aged 18+ on Google AI Plus, Pro or Ultra. It is not free. The Verge notes it arrives as Apple previews tighter rules in a macOS beta for apps that ask for full disk access.
stories.matters: A lot of office work lives in desktop apps with no connector: old finance tools, design software, internal portals. An agent that can drive those apps while you keep working turns dozens of repetitive clicks into one instruction.
stories.imply: It is for personal accounts only, so most company Macs managed through Google Workspace will not get it yet. Anything that can click through your apps can also make mistakes in them, so keep approvals on and limit which apps it can touch.
uses: Fill in the same web form from a folder of PDFs, one file at a time, and approve each submission.
Rename, sort and file a month of downloaded receipts into the right folders.
Pull last week’s numbers from three dashboards into a short Slides deck for a Monday meeting.
stories.example: An operations assistant asks Gemini to read 20 supplier PDFs and enter each package’s weight and delivery address into a courier’s quote form, approving each quote before it is sent.
stories.audience: Mac users on paid Google AI plans in the US, freelancers and small-business owners with repetitive desktop chores.
stories.watch: When it reaches Workspace business accounts and other countries, and how Apple’s new full disk access rules affect agents like this.

source.title: Google: Let Gemini tackle repetitive chores on your Mac, 19 November 2026
source.quote: You remain in control by approving every action and choosing exactly which apps Gemini can access.

stories.theme: Anthropic’s shares opened 34% above the IPO price on day one and closed up 17%, at $97.17
stories.changed: Anthropic, the maker of Claude, started trading on Nasdaq as ANT on 19 November 2026, a day after pricing its IPO at $83 a share. CNBC reports the stock opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17, 17% above the IPO price. More than 846 million shares changed hands, against 522 million on SpaceX’s first day in June, and at the close Anthropic had a fully diluted market value of roughly $1.8 trillion, behind only Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet, Amazon and SpaceX among US companies, according to CNBC. The listing raised $81.3 billion, the largest IPO on record. The wider market was weaker: the BBC reports the Nasdaq Composite closed down nearly 2.3%, with Alphabet and Amazon, both large Anthropic shareholders, falling 3% and 3.9%.
stories.matters: Claude’s maker now answers to public shareholders every quarter. Its results, spending and pricing decisions will be public and scrutinised, which matters to any team that builds on Claude.
stories.imply: One day of trading says little about the company. The BBC notes a first-day jump is often followed by a fall in the weeks after. For customers, nothing about Claude changes because of the listing itself.
uses: If your team depends on Claude, note when Anthropic reports results and read what it says about prices and capacity.
Finance teams: check whether your company’s pension or ESOP funds now hold Anthropic, directly or through index funds later.
Keep a second model tested for your key jobs, whatever the share price does.
stories.example: A product lead adds Anthropic’s first earnings date to the team calendar and plans a review of Claude costs and limits that week.
stories.audience: Teams that build on Claude, investors, and anyone tracking how the AI industry is valued.
stories.watch: The first quarterly report as a public company, the share price once the opening excitement fades, and whether other AI labs list next.

stories.theme: OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Accounting: a plugin that reconciles, drafts invoice entries and prepares month-end reports for you to review
stories.changed: OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Accounting, with an Accounting plugin in the ChatGPT desktop app for macOS and Windows. It helps reconcile transactions, draft invoice and receipt entries with suggested account coding, prepare month-end reports in your own Excel template, and gather audit support, flagging unclear items for review. Partner plugins connect it to BILL, Campfire, FreshBooks, Oracle NetSuite, Oracle QuickStart, QuickBooks Online, Rillet and Xero, and computer use lets it work in apps without a plugin. OpenAI’s help page says the plugin is free to install; Business members can install it themselves, while Enterprise admins must approve it first. OpenAI tells users to review records, calculations and coding before approving any entry or report. On 19 November FreshBooks said its connection is read-only, so ChatGPT can answer questions from live data but cannot change anything in the account.
stories.matters: Month-end close is slow, repetitive and full of matching work. A tool that drafts entries and points to the record behind every figure can cut hours, while the accountant keeps the final say.
stories.imply: Customer time savings on OpenAI’s page are the customers’ own estimates. Each partner plugin has its own permissions: some can only read, others can post entries, so check which one you are connecting before you let it write.
uses: Give it a bank statement and the ledger for the same month and ask for matches, duplicates and missing items, with the source row for each.
Draft entries from a folder of supplier invoices with your coding rules, and review them before posting.
Save your month-end report format as a reusable skill and run it each month on new records.
stories.example: A small firm’s bookkeeper asks ChatGPT to list every November invoice still missing a receipt in FreshBooks and draft reminder emails to the clients who owe money.
stories.audience: Accountants, bookkeepers, controllers and small-business owners using ChatGPT Business, Enterprise or other eligible plans.
stories.watch: Which partner plugins allow posting entries, how firms handle review and audit trails, and whether rivals ship similar accounting agents.

source.title: OpenAI: ChatGPT for Accounting
source.quote: Review supporting records, calculations, and suggested coding before approving entries or reports.

stories.theme: Meta staff testing its Muse agent saw it read Signal messages and show chats and bank balances that were not theirs, Reuters reports
stories.changed: Reuters reported on 18 November, from more than two dozen internal posts, that Meta employees testing Muse, the company’s personal AI agent, saw it send messages about childcare requests, career advice, product orders and bank balances that were not theirs. One employee said Muse reminded her to reply to her sister on Signal even though she did not recall giving it access to other apps. Another said it booked a short-term rental without permission, PYMNTS reports, citing Reuters. Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts called the examples “isolated incidents”, said Muse can only use other apps with permissions people explicitly grant, and said many of the apparent mix-ups were hallucinations that have been fixed; employees were told built-in prompts pushing the agent to engage between sessions had caused them. Reuters said it could not establish whether Muse was showing other people’s real data or making it up. Muse has had more than 10 million downloads since its September launch, according to Reuters.
stories.matters: Personal agents get deep access to messages, accounts and money. Whether this was leaked data or invented data, an agent sending bank balances and private chats unprompted is the kind of failure that erodes trust fast.
stories.imply: Meta says employees test different versions from the public. Still, it is a reminder to check which apps and accounts any agent can reach, and to switch off access you do not need.
uses: Open your AI agent’s settings and list every app and account it is connected to. Remove what you do not use.
Keep purchases and bookings behind your own approval, with a spending cap.
At work, ask IT which personal AI agents are allowed on devices that hold company messages.
stories.example: A team lead finds her personal agent can read her work chat app on her phone and removes that permission before the next client call.
stories.audience: Anyone using a personal AI agent on their phone or computer, and IT and security teams setting device policy.
stories.watch: Whether Meta publishes what caused the mix-ups, any regulator questions, and changes to how Muse asks for app access.

source.title: TechCrunch: Meta’s AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations and could be exposing private data, report says, 19 November 2026
source.quote: This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this.

stories.theme: The largest US school districts may drop Google Search after Google said schools cannot switch off its AI without losing Search
stories.changed: New York, Los Angeles and Chicago schools are considering alternatives to Google Search, The Verge reported on 18 November, citing The New York Times. Google said that from next year schools will not be able to turn off Gemini-powered features without also turning off Search; its vice president of education, Chris Phillips, said schools that turn off the AI features “will not have access to Search”. New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said the city will explore other search options if Google does not reconsider, and Chicago told Google it will look elsewhere if it cannot offer Search without AI. In a statement to The Verge, Google said it is piloting Guided Learning in Search this month to walk students through problems step by step, and that next year Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools choose which services to enable.
stories.matters: This is the first big test of whether an organisation can buy search without AI answers. The same question is coming for companies that want to control where staff see AI-generated content.
stories.imply: Schools are deeply tied to Google through Classroom and Chromebooks, so a full switch is hard. Expect pressure on Google to offer a clear no-AI option for education, and possibly for businesses.
uses: IT admins: check which AI features your Google Workspace or browser setup turns on by default, and who can change them.
Teachers: test a no-AI search option on school devices before the next term.
Policy teams: write down where staff or students may and may not see AI answers.
stories.example: A district IT lead sets up a test group of Chromebooks with a search engine that lets AI answers be switched off and asks teachers for feedback.
stories.audience: School districts, education IT teams, teachers and parents, and IT admins in any organisation using Google.
stories.watch: Whether Google changes its position before next year’s controls update, and which search providers schools pick.

source.title: The Verge: The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search, 18 November 2026
source.quote: If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.

stories.theme: OpenAI’s Codex agents now investigate slowdowns in ChatGPT, propose fixes for engineers and check the fix worked
stories.changed: On 19 November 2026 OpenAI described its Performance Factory, a cloud system in which Codex agents find and fix performance problems in ChatGPT. In its first workflow, a performance alert opens a task, an agent investigates the slowdown, records what it found and proposes a fix for an engineer to review; after the fix is deployed, another agent checks whether performance is back to normal. OpenAI says that in just over three months this Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and found the root cause of more than 600, about 17 automated investigations a day. The system has four parts: a task tracker with configurable workflows, a loop that hands ready work to agents, an API that runs Codex in the cloud, and subscriptions that wake agents when something changes, such as a GitHub review comment or a finished deployment.
stories.matters: It shows a practical pattern for agents at work: a clear trigger, a written process, a person approving the fix, and an agent checking the result. That pattern fits support queues, finance checks and operations, not just code.
stories.imply: These are OpenAI’s own figures about its own system. Engineers still review every fix. Copying the idea needs good alerts and clear task stages first.
uses: Pick one recurring alert your team handles and write down its stages: investigate, cause found, fix proposed, resolved.
Let an agent draft the investigation notes for each alert, and keep a person approving any change.
Add a follow-up check a day after each fix to confirm the problem did not come back.
stories.example: A web team sets up an agent that opens a ticket when page load time jumps, lists the code changes deployed that day and suggests the most likely cause for an engineer to confirm.
stories.audience: Engineering managers, site reliability and operations teams, and anyone designing agent workflows.
stories.watch: Whether OpenAI turns this into a product for Codex customers, and how many fixes agents propose that engineers accept.

source.title: OpenAI: How OpenAI’s Performance Factory keeps ChatGPT fast, 19 November 2026
source.quote: In just over three months, the Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root caused over 600 cases.
